AMOS ALONZO STAGG, BETA '88, STILL
AN ACTIVE FOOTBALL COACH AT
THE AGE OF 74
STARTING
his forty-seventh year as a football coach finds
Brother Amos Alonzo Stagg, Beta '88, truly the grand old man
of football, "fit as a fiddle" in his own words.
Described by sports writers as "football's eternal freshman,"
Brother Stagg, who was seventy-four in August declares he intends
to coach until he is 100 if he keeps on feeling the way he does now.
In fact he recently told newspaper men that if he felt any better he
would turn out for the team himself.
A small, quick, silver haired gentleman. Brother Stagg gets up
at six every morning, walks and runs two miles before breakfast.
Two or three times a week he plays tennis.
Fourth Season on Pacific Coast
Some weeks ago he rounded up his College of the Pacific boys at
Stockton, California, and started to make another good team for the
institution. We regret that The Diamond goes to press too early to
describe the results he has achieved this year. This will be his fourth
season with the Pacific Coast institution.
In 1890, Brother Stagg started a football coaching career which
cannot be equaled in American grid history. His first assignment was
with Springfield (Massachusetts) College where he remained for two
years. Then he moved on to the University of Chicago where he
remained for forty-one years, establishing for himseK the right to
be mentioned in the same breath with such football immortals as
KJiute Rockne, Pop Warner, Fielding Yost, and others.
Almost half a century ago. Brother Stagg got certain ideas about
the great American college game, and through all these years they
haven't changed very much.
He thinks football is the finest of all sports, the true character
builder, something which fits into the life of young men.
Recently he made the following remarks about the game to the
Associated Press :

"It teaches unity, team spirit, breeds courage, combats selfish
ness, and improves youth physically and mentally.
"Football is a game for individuals but not for individualism.
"I'd rather have one ordinary player who thinks of the team first
rather than eleven who think of it last.
"No player of mine can use liquor, tobacco or profanity, and ex
pect to remain on the squad; they don't mix with football.
"Ail-American selections are all right, but they serve no purpose.
Nevertheless, as end at Yale, I am proud to have been named for the
first All-American team in 1889.
"There is really nothing new in football. Criss crosses were in
vogue in the 80's. We call them reverses now.
"The boy who plays a clean hard game will always have his self
respect.
"The cheater only cheats himself in the long run."

DR. ROSWELL GRAY HAM, EPSILON '14,
NAMED PRESIDENT OF MOUNT
HOLYOKE COLLEGE
NOW A PROFESSOR OF ENGLISH LITERATURE
AT YALE, HE BECOMES THE FIRST MAN
TO HEAD THE MASSACHUSETTS
INSTITUTION
ROSWELL
GRAY HAM, Epsilon '14, has joined the ranks of
Psi U's heading women's colleges. The ranks are not very
large, however, as Dr. Henry Noble MacCracken, Delta '00,
president of Vassar College, is the only other one in the "Ranks" as
far as we know. Brother Ham will take over the executive duties at
Mount Holyoke College in October 1937.
Dr. Ham, who is at present associate professor of English litera
ture at Yale will be the third president of the Massachusetts college,
which was founded as a seminary in 1836, and became an institution
of higher learning in 1893.
Chosen After Long Search
According to a statement issued by the Board of Trustees of the
college. Brother Ham was chosen after more than a year of intensive
search to succeed Dr. Mary E. WooUey who has been president of the
college since the turn of the century. The fact that he is an extremely
handsome individual may or may not have had anything to do with
his selection, but the fact that he has established himself as an ex
tremely able executive and scholar had much to do with the choice.
The college authorities shattered a number of precedents when
they chose Dr. Ham. In the first place he is not a New Englander,
but a Californian. In the second place, he is naturally not a graduate
of Mount Holyoke. But on the other hand, the college has always
seen fit to break tradition if the circumstances warrant.
Professor Ham is considered one of the most distinguished
teachers in Yale University. He is in charge of the course in English
literature for freshmen and sophomores, one of the key courses for

undergraduates. He also directs the work of honor students in the
upper classes and gives two courses in the graduate school. In the
course of his career he has acquired first-hand experience in the edu
cation of women, first in the posts he held at the University of Wash
ington and the University of California, and latterly as a faculty
member of Albertus Magnus College, New Haven.
As a scholar. Professor Ham has already obtained an enviable
reputation. He is an authority on Dryden, and his publications have
won him high standing among the English scholars in the United
States. As executive fellow of Jonathan Edwards College since its
inception in 1933, he has shared with the master the administration
of the college. As chairman of the freshman year counselors of Yale
University, he has acquired additional training as an administrator
in a post involving close contact with students and faculty. This
combination of achievement as teacher, scholar and administrative
officer fits him admirably for the presidency of a college of the liberal
arts.
Born in California
Dr. Ham, who is forty-five years old, was bom in Lemoore, Cali
fornia. He was graduated from the University of California in
1914, and the next year became an instructor of English at the
University of Washington, returning to California in that capacity
in 1916.
At the outbreak of the World War he enlisted in the Marine
Corps and served overseas, first as a lieutenant and then as a cap
tain. On demobilization he returned to devote his time to liberal arts
education. In making this decision he rejected the pffer of the Strat
ford Players, of England, to join the company as a Shakesperian
actor.
He entered the Yale Graduate School in 1920, and received his
doctorate in English literature in 1925, and, while studying, served
as an instructor in English, becoming an assistant professor in 1925,
and an associate professor in 1934. In 1926, Dr. Ham was elected to
the Elizabethan Club at Yale and in 1926-27 won the Sterling Fel
lowship.
